title: The Long Discourses
hookLine: thirty-four long discourses, many set as stories and conversations

lines: A KING ON A MOONLIT ROOF.
cards: A king on his palace roof on a full-moon night, asking his ministers which teacher to visit. A brahmin with hundreds of animals tied up for a sacrifice.
A monk climbing through heaven after heaven with a question no god can answer. The Buddha's last journey, step by step, to the grove where he lay down for the last time.
These are all in one collection, and it's only thirty-four discourses long.

teach.b: The Pali name is Digha Nikaya, the long collection; digha just means long.

teach.h: THREE PARTS: MORALITY, GREAT, THE REST
teach.b: Thirty-four discourses, some as long as a short book, in three parts. The first, thirteen discourses, is named for morality, because each one contains the same long passage on a monk's conduct.
The second, the great division, holds the big set pieces: the Buddha's final days, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness.
The third gathers the rest, including the advice to a young householder named Sigala on how to treat parents, teachers, spouse, friends and workers.

Where the Middle-Length Sayings often talk to monks, the long ones often talk to outsiders: kings, wealthy brahmins, wandering philosophers, a curious householder. Many are stories with a setting and a plot.

Someone arrives with a question, a challenge, sometimes a grudge, and leaves changed, or not. Some scholars suggest this collection was especially suited to presenting the teaching to people who weren't yet followers.
That's a theory, and others weigh it differently.

teach.h: DIALOGUES, TAKEN A PIECE AT A TIME
teach.b: In English, an early translation came from Thomas Rhys Davids, later joined by Caroline Rhys Davids, under the title Dialogues of the Buddha, starting in 1899.

That name fits. Over the next weeks we'll read the first thirteen in order: praise and blame, the net of views, a king's moonlit ride, a proud young brahmin, a sacrifice with no blood, the line of the blind.

how: The Digha Nikaya is the first of the five collections of discourses in the Pali Canon; Theravada monastics study it, and some of its discourses, like the one on the foundations of mindfulness, are recited and widely taught.

games.q: you open the long collection for the first time. where does this path start reading?
o: the first thirteen discourses, in order.
games.why: over the coming weeks the path reads the first thirteen in order, starting tomorrow with praise and blame.

practice: Hear a few titles the way you'd read a menu: the supreme net, the fruits of the contemplative life, the great discourse on the final passing, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the advice to Sigala.
Notice which one pulls at you, even a little, without deciding why, and rest with the breath.
